title: Vomiting and Weakness in a University Student
objective: Students recognise severe hyperglycaemia in a young adult with type 1 diabetes who has been vomiting, interpret compensatory breathing, prioritize deficient fluid volume as the nursing diagnosis before the results confirm diabetic ketoacidosis, plan hourly fluid-balance monitoring, follow the ward protocol when glucose falls without stopping insulin, judge restored fluid volume by pulse, mucous membranes and urine output, teach sick-day rules, and delegate safely during the move back to subcutaneous insulin.
population: Young adult, 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes
setting: Medical ward, regional hospital, Trinidad and Tobago
endpoint: Ketoacidosis resolved and the client transferred back to usual subcutaneous insulin, with sick-day teaching before discharge

opening.narrative: Akeem, a 22-year-old university student, is admitted directly to the medical ward from the district health centre. Akeem's mother brought Akeem to the health centre after two days of vomiting, crampy abdominal pain and weakness. The mother says, "Akeem can't keep anything down, not even water, and has been getting up all night to pass water." History includes type 1 diabetes since age 15, treated with NPH and regular insulin by injection before breakfast and before dinner. No known drug allergies. Akeem lives at home with family in Chaguanas. At the health centre an IV cannula was inserted and 0.9% sodium chloride was started; it is still running on arrival.

stages.narrative: The nurse completes the admission assessment.

assessment.finding: Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Says, "I just feel weak and tired."
Capillary refill 3 seconds. Radial pulses present and equal.
Breathing regular. Chest clear on auscultation bilaterally.
Generalised abdominal tenderness, no guarding. Vomited about 100 mL of clear fluid on arrival.
Reports passing large amounts of urine for three days.
Moves all limbs equally. Generalised weakness; walks to the bathroom with assistance.
Lips and tongue dry. Skin turgor reduced on the forearm. Skin warm and dry.
Mother at the bedside. Akeem is cooperative and worried about missing university classes.

stages.narrative: On questioning, Akeem tells the nurse, "I stopped my insulin two days ago because I wasn't eating anything." The nurse reassesses. The ward's bedside ketone meter is on loan to the emergency department and has been sent for. The physician, informed by telephone, asks for urgent blood tests, and the nurse sends the samples at 2:40 pm.

assessment.finding: Takes longer to answer questions but remains oriented to person, place and time.
Capillary refill 3 seconds. Radial pulses present and equal.
Fruity odour on the breath. Chest clear on auscultation bilaterally. No cough.
Generalised abdominal tenderness, no guarding. Nauseated; no further vomiting since arrival.
Passed about 350 mL of pale urine since admission.
Moves all limbs equally. Generalised weakness.
Lips and tongue dry. Skin turgor reduced on the forearm. Skin warm and dry.
Mother at the bedside. Akeem is cooperative with care.

stages.narrative: The results are reported and the physician reviews Akeem on the ward and confirms diabetic ketoacidosis. Prescriptions: continue 0.9% sodium chloride IV at the prescribed rate; a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion of 6.4 units/hr (weight 64 kg) to start at 3:30 pm; hourly capillary glucose and blood ketones; electrolytes repeated 2 hours after the insulin starts. The ward's physician-signed IV insulin protocol directs the nurse to start 10% dextrose at 125 mL/hr through a second line once capillary glucose falls below 250 mg/dL. Any change to the insulin rate needs a physician's prescription.

medications.name: Soluble (regular) insulin 50 units in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride
10% dextrose
medications.frequency: continuous, once capillary glucose is below 250 mg/dL (ward protocol)

stages.narrative: The insulin infusion has run at 6.4 units/hr since 3:30 pm. At 5:30 pm the repeat potassium was 4.6 mmol/L, and potassium chloride was added to the 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed. Akeem has stopped vomiting and has taken sips of water. The 7:00 pm checks are back.

assessment.finding: Alert, answers questions promptly.
Capillary refill 2 seconds. Radial pulses strong and equal.
Breathing regular. Faint fruity odour on the breath. Chest clear on auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen soft, mildly tender, no guarding. No vomiting since 4:00 pm; taking sips of water.
Urine output 240 mL over the past 3 hours.
Moves all limbs equally. Sitting up in bed unaided.
Lips slightly dry. Skin turgor brisk on the forearm.
Mother at the bedside. Akeem asks when it will be possible to go home.

medications.name: 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride 40 mmol/L

stages.narrative: The insulin infusion, 10% dextrose and 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium ran overnight as prescribed. Akeem slept for most of the night.

assessment.finding: Alert and oriented, conversing normally.
Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Radial pulses strong and equal.
Breathing regular. No odour on the breath. Chest clear on auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen soft and non-tender. Asking for breakfast.
Urine output about 70 mL/hr overnight.
Moves all limbs equally. Walked to the bathroom unaided.
Lips and tongue moist. Skin turgor brisk on the forearm.
Rested after sleeping most of the night. Asks about going home.

medications.name: 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride 40 mmol/L

stages.narrative: The physician prescribes Akeem's usual subcutaneous NPH and regular insulin with breakfast, and the insulin infusion to stop one hour after the subcutaneous dose. The nurse gives the dose and Akeem eats breakfast. Akeem says, "I thought that if I wasn't eating, I shouldn't take my insulin. What am I supposed to do the next time I get sick?"

The insulin infusion was stopped at 9:30 am as prescribed. The nurse is responsible for six clients this morning and works with one nursing assistant. Several of Akeem's tasks remain before lunch, and discharge home is planned for Day 3 with a diabetes clinic appointment.

questions.stem: Which finding should the nurse recognize as most important to follow up, given Akeem's history?

options.label: A
options.text: Tympanic temperature of 37.5°C

options.label: B
options.text: Generalised abdominal tenderness

options.label: C
options.text: Capillary glucose of 486 mg/dL

options.label: D
options.text: Pulse of 116/min at rest in bed

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Akeem has type 1 diabetes and has been vomiting for two days. A capillary glucose of 486 mg/dL is not explained by a stomach illness alone; it signals a serious lack of insulin, and in type 1 diabetes that raises the risk of ketone build-up. It needs follow-up now (ketone testing and informing the physician). The fast pulse, dry mouth and poor skin turgor need close monitoring, but they are explained by the vomiting and passing large amounts of urine; the glucose is the cue that explains why the losses are so large.

distractor_rationales.A: A temperature of 37.5°C is only slightly raised and fits a minor infection or dehydration. It is worth rechecking but does not change the immediate plan.
distractor_rationales.B: Generalised tenderness without guarding fits two days of vomiting and is also common when glucose is very high. It needs reassessment, but it is not the finding that points to the dangerous problem.
distractor_rationales.D: A pulse of 116/min with dry mucous membranes and reduced turgor is expected after two days of vomiting and polyuria, and IV fluid has been started. It needs close monitoring, but the glucose explains why the fluid loss happened and what else may be developing.

questions.self_test: The pulse of 116/min matches the fluid loss from vomiting and polyuria, whereas a glucose of 486 mg/dL in type 1 diabetes signals the insulin lack that is causing it.

meta.priority_principle: Follow up the cue the presenting illness does not explain
meta.prerequisites: Normal blood glucose range; signs of dehydration; insulin action
meta.suggested_review: Assessment of the client with diabetes who is unwell

questions.stem: How should the nurse interpret the significance of the change in Akeem's breathing?

options.label: A
options.text: The breathing pattern is removing carbon dioxide to offset acid

options.label: B
options.text: The breathing pattern reflects anxiety about vomiting and admission

options.label: C
options.text: The breathing pattern suggests vomit was inhaled into the lungs

options.label: D
options.text: The breathing pattern shows the IV fluid is overloading the circulation

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Without insulin, Akeem's body has been breaking down fat for energy for two days, producing acidic ketones (the fruity breath odour). The rise from 22/min to 30/min, deep and regular, with a clear chest and SpO2 of 98%, is the lungs blowing off carbon dioxide to reduce the acid load. Together with the slower responses, it shows the acid build-up is getting worse.

distractor_rationales.B: Anxiety can speed up breathing, but it is usually shallow and is not accompanied by a fruity breath odour and slower mental responses. Putting it down to anxiety would miss a worsening acid build-up.
distractor_rationales.C: Inhaling vomit is a real risk after repeated vomiting, which is why this is tempting. But the chest is clear and SpO2 is 98%; aspiration would usually bring crackles, cough or falling oxygen saturation.
distractor_rationales.D: Fluid overload is a risk with IV therapy, but Akeem is dehydrated, the blood pressure is still 102/64 mm Hg and the chest is clear, so the breathing change is not from too much fluid.

questions.self_test: Anxiety explains fast breathing but not deep breaths with a fruity odour and slower responses after two days without insulin.

meta.priority_principle: Link new cues to the underlying physiology
meta.prerequisites: Acid-base balance; role of the lungs in removing carbon dioxide; ketone production

questions.stem: Before the blood results return, which nursing diagnosis should the nurse prioritize for Akeem?

options.label: A
options.text: Ineffective breathing pattern related to compensation for acid build-up as evidenced by deep respirations of 30/min

options.label: B
options.text: Risk for electrolyte imbalance related to losses of potassium and sodium in vomit and urine

options.label: C
options.text: Deficient knowledge related to unfamiliarity with sick-day rules as evidenced by stopping insulin when not eating

options.label: D
options.text: Deficient fluid volume related to osmotic diuresis and vomiting as evidenced by a pulse of 118/min and a dry mouth

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Deficient fluid volume is an actual problem that threatens circulation now. Two days of vomiting and glucose-driven urine loss (osmotic diuresis; 350 mL more since admission) have left Akeem with a pulse rising from 116 to 118/min, blood pressure falling to 102/64 mm Hg, capillary refill of 3 seconds, a dry mouth and reduced skin turgor. Restoring volume comes first by airway, breathing, circulation: it supports blood pressure, restores kidney perfusion so glucose and ketones can be cleared, and must be under way before potassium can be replaced safely.

distractor_rationales.A: The airway-breathing-circulation order makes this tempting, but the deep, rapid breathing is the lungs compensating for acid, as Q2 showed. It is effective: SpO2 is 98% on room air and the chest is clear. It settles as fluid and insulin correct the acidosis and is not a problem the nurse corrects directly.
distractor_rationales.B: Potassium and sodium are being lost and will shift once insulin starts, so this risk is real and will be monitored. But it is a risk diagnosis with no results yet, and an actual circulatory problem comes before a risk one.
distractor_rationales.C: Stopping insulin because of not eating shows a real knowledge gap, and it caused this episode. It is addressed with sick-day teaching once Akeem is stable, not ahead of a circulatory problem.

questions.self_test: The deep breathing looks like a breathing problem, but it is an effective compensation with SpO2 98% and a clear chest, whereas the fluid deficit is an actual threat to circulation.

meta.subtopic: Priority nursing diagnosis in a hyperglycaemic crisis
meta.priority_principle: Airway, breathing, circulation: an actual circulatory problem before a compensatory or risk problem
meta.prerequisites: Nursing diagnosis structure; signs of hypovolaemia; osmotic diuresis; respiratory compensation
meta.suggested_review: Nursing care planning for the client with diabetic ketoacidosis

questions.stem: As the insulin infusion begins, which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care for Akeem's priority problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Encourage at least 250 mL of oral fluid every hour while awake

options.label: B
options.text: Record intake and urine output hourly with pulse and blood pressure

options.label: C
options.text: Weigh Akeem each morning to judge how well fluid is being replaced

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the IV fluid rate whenever the pulse stays above 100/min

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The priority problem is deficient fluid volume, and fluid is being replaced IV at a prescribed rate while insulin starts. Hourly intake and urine output, with pulse and blood pressure, show whether the circulation is recovering (output steady while the pulse falls), pick up a falling output or signs of overload early so the physician can be informed, and confirm that Akeem is passing urine, which is needed before potassium is added to the fluid as the level of 5.8 mmol/L falls on insulin.

distractor_rationales.A: Oral fluid will help later, but Akeem is still nauseated and vomited on arrival, so large oral volumes are likely to come back up. Replacement at this stage is IV; sips can be offered once vomiting settles.
distractor_rationales.C: Daily weight is a sound fluid-balance measure, which is why it is tempting, but once a day is far too infrequent while litres are given and lost within hours. It cannot guide care over the next few hours.
distractor_rationales.D: Watching the pulse is right, but the fluid rate is prescribed, and changing it is outside the nurse's authority. A persistent tachycardia is reported to the physician, not corrected by adjusting the infusion.

questions.self_test: Daily weight does reflect fluid balance, but with litres given and lost within hours only hourly intake, output and vital signs show the response in time to act.

meta.subtopic: Fluid balance monitoring in diabetic ketoacidosis
meta.priority_principle: Plan monitoring that measures the priority problem often enough to act on it
meta.prerequisites: Expected urine output (about 0.5 mL/kg/hr); signs of hypovolaemia and fluid overload; potassium and kidney function
meta.suggested_review: Fluid balance charting and hourly urine output

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse perform now?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop the insulin infusion and recheck glucose in one hour

options.label: B
options.text: Give the usual subcutaneous insulin and stop the infusion

options.label: C
options.text: Start the dextrose infusion and keep insulin at the same rate

options.label: D
options.text: Offer sweet juice by mouth and recheck glucose in one hour

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The capillary glucose is now 236 mg/dL, below the protocol's 250 mg/dL point, so the nurse starts 10% dextrose at 125 mL/hr as the ward protocol directs. Blood ketones are still 2.4 mmol/L, so the ketoacidosis has not resolved, and the insulin must continue at the prescribed rate to switch off ketone production; the dextrose lets it continue without causing hypoglycaemia. Only a physician's prescription can change the insulin rate.

distractor_rationales.A: Stopping insulin because the glucose has come down is the classic error. Ketones are still 2.4 mmol/L, so ketone production would restart and the acidosis would return; the protocol also does not allow the nurse to change the insulin.
distractor_rationales.B: Returning to subcutaneous insulin is the right step later, once the ketoacidosis has resolved and Akeem is eating. With ketones at 2.4 mmol/L it is too early, and the switch needs a physician's prescription.
distractor_rationales.D: Akeem has only just stopped vomiting and is managing sips, so oral juice is unreliable, and it is not what the protocol directs. Waiting an hour leaves the glucose falling with the insulin still running.

questions.self_test: Oral juice tries to protect against a low glucose, but it is unreliable after vomiting, and the protocol's dextrose infusion is what allows insulin to keep clearing ketones safely.

meta.subtopic: IV insulin infusion protocol in DKA
meta.priority_principle: Treat the ketosis, not the glucose number
meta.prerequisites: Insulin suppresses ketone production; scope of a ward protocol
meta.suggested_review: Adding dextrose during IV insulin therapy for DKA

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that care for Akeem's priority nursing diagnosis has been effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulse 86/min, moist tongue, urine output 70 mL/hr

options.label: B
options.text: Blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L with a venous pH of 7.35

options.label: C
options.text: Capillary glucose of 168 mg/dL before breakfast

options.label: D
options.text: Asking for breakfast, with a soft abdomen

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The priority nursing diagnosis was deficient fluid volume, so its outcome is a restored circulating volume. After a night of IV fluid with hourly intake and output, the pulse has fallen from 118 to 86/min, the lips and tongue are moist instead of dry, and urine output is a steady 70 mL/hr (about 1 mL/kg/hr). With glucose now 168 mg/dL, too low to drive glucose into the urine, that output reflects good kidney perfusion rather than osmotic diuresis.

distractor_rationales.B: Ketones of 0.4 mmol/L and a pH of 7.35 show the ketoacidosis has resolved, which matters for stopping the insulin infusion, but they measure the acid problem, not whether the fluid deficit has been corrected.
distractor_rationales.C: A lower glucose reduces glucose-driven urine loss, but glucose was already 236 mg/dL yesterday evening while Akeem's lips were still slightly dry, so it cannot show that volume has been restored.
distractor_rationales.D: Appetite and a soft abdomen are encouraging and matter for restarting subcutaneous insulin, but they say little about circulating volume.

questions.self_test: Ketones of 0.4 mmol/L and a pH of 7.35 show the acidosis has cleared, but the priority nursing diagnosis was the fluid deficit, which is measured by pulse, mucous membranes and urine output.

meta.priority_principle: Evaluate the expected outcome of the priority nursing diagnosis
meta.prerequisites: Signs of adequate hydration; expected urine output; effect of glucose on urine output
meta.suggested_review: Expected outcomes for deficient fluid volume

questions.stem: Which instruction is most important for the nurse to include in Akeem's teaching?

options.label: A
options.text: Halve each insulin dose on days you are unable to eat

options.label: B
options.text: Rest in bed and check your glucose once each morning

options.label: C
options.text: Go to the health centre whenever you have a cold or fever

options.label: D
options.text: Keep taking insulin and check glucose and ketones every 4 hours

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: This episode began when Akeem stopped insulin because of not eating. Illness raises stress hormones, which push glucose up and drive ketone production even without food, so insulin must continue during illness. Checking glucose and ketones about every 4 hours lets Akeem spot rising levels early and seek help before ketoacidosis develops again.

distractor_rationales.A: Halving the dose sounds like a cautious middle ground, but illness usually raises the insulin requirement. Cutting the dose could start the same ketone build-up that caused this admission.
distractor_rationales.B: Rest is reasonable, but one glucose check a day is far too infrequent during illness, and it does not include ketone testing, which would have shown the problem early.
distractor_rationales.C: Seeking help is important when vomiting persists or ketones rise, but going in for every cold does not teach Akeem to manage illness at home and would not prevent a recurrence.

questions.self_test: Halving the dose seems safer when not eating, but illness raises insulin needs, so a reduced dose can start ketone production again.

meta.priority_principle: Teach the behaviour that caused the episode
meta.prerequisites: Effect of stress hormones on glucose; insulin and ketone production
meta.suggested_review: Sick-day management for clients taking insulin

questions.stem: Which task for Akeem may the nurse appropriately delegate to the nursing assistant?

options.label: A
options.text: Disconnect the stopped insulin infusion from the cannula

options.label: B
options.text: Measure and record oral intake and urine output on the chart

options.label: C
options.text: Check that Akeem can explain the sick-day plan correctly

options.label: D
options.text: Give Akeem a snack whenever Akeem reports feeling shaky

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Measuring and recording intake and output is a routine, predictable task with a standard method, for a client who is now stable on subcutaneous insulin. It is within a nursing assistant's role, and the nurse still reviews the totals and acts on them.

distractor_rationales.A: Handling an IV line and cannula used for an insulin infusion is IV therapy and remains the registered nurse's responsibility, even when the infusion has stopped.
distractor_rationales.C: Checking whether teaching has been understood is evaluation of learning, which needs the registered nurse's judgement and may lead to re-teaching.
distractor_rationales.D: Giving a snack is something a nursing assistant often does, which is why this is tempting. But shakiness after the insulin infusion stops may signal hypoglycaemia; it needs a glucose check and assessment by the registered nurse first, and a snack alone may be too little or delay treatment.

questions.self_test: Checking that Akeem can explain the plan seems simple, but it is evaluation of teaching, which needs the registered nurse's judgement.

meta.priority_principle: Delegate stable, routine tasks; keep assessment, teaching evaluation and IV therapy
meta.prerequisites: Principles of delegation; role of the nursing assistant

pathophysiology:
## Pathophysiology teaching

**Normal physiology.** Insulin moves glucose into muscle and fat cells, stops the liver releasing glucose, and stops fat being broken down. In type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes almost no insulin, so these effects depend entirely on injected insulin.

**What happened to Akeem.** An illness with vomiting (probably a stomach upset) stopped Akeem eating, and Akeem then stopped the insulin. Illness also raises stress hormones (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline), which raise glucose and fat breakdown further. Without insulin:
- Glucose cannot enter cells and the liver keeps releasing it, so glucose climbed to 486 mg/dL.
- Glucose spills into the urine and draws water with it (osmotic diuresis), causing polyuria, thirst, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia and a raised urea and creatinine. Vomiting adds to the fluid and electrolyte loss.
- Fat is broken down and the liver turns the fatty acids into ketones. Ketones are acids, so bicarbonate is used up and the pH falls (7.16, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L). The lungs try to compensate by blowing off carbon dioxide, giving deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, and acetone gives the breath a fruity odour. Acidosis also causes abdominal pain, vomiting and drowsiness.
- Potassium is lost in urine and vomit, but acidosis and insulin lack keep potassium outside the cells, so the serum level (5.8 mmol/L) hides a low total body potassium.

**Priority nursing diagnosis.** Deficient fluid volume related to osmotic diuresis and vomiting, as evidenced by a pulse of 118/min, falling blood pressure, slow capillary refill, a dry mouth and reduced skin turgor. It came first by airway, breathing, circulation: the airway was clear, the deep breathing was an effective compensation (SpO2 98%), and circulation was what was failing. Restoring volume also restores kidney perfusion, which clears glucose and ketones and must be in place before potassium is given. The physician's working diagnosis, confirmed by the results, was diabetic ketoacidosis.

**Why each decision mattered.**
- Q1: the glucose was the cue the stomach illness did not explain, and it pointed to insulin lack as the cause of the fluid loss.
- Q2: reading the deep breathing as compensation for acid, not anxiety, aspiration or overload, showed the problem was getting worse.
- Q3: choosing deficient fluid volume over the breathing pattern, electrolyte risk or knowledge gap put the actual threat to circulation first, before the results arrived.
- Q4: hourly intake, urine output, pulse and blood pressure measure the priority problem often enough to act on it, and confirm urine flow before potassium is added as insulin drives the serum level down.
- Q5: glucose falls faster than ketones clear. Adding dextrose lets insulin continue until ketone production is switched off; stopping insulin when glucose falls lets the acidosis return.
- Q6: the outcome of the priority nursing diagnosis is judged by pulse, mucous membranes and urine output; ketones and pH show the acidosis has cleared, a separate outcome.
- Q7 and Q8: sick-day teaching targets the knowledge gap that started this episode, and delegating only routine, stable tasks (such as recording intake and output) keeps assessment, IV therapy and evaluation of teaching with the registered nurse during the move back to subcutaneous insulin, when hypoglycaemia or rebound ketosis can occur.

**Moving back to subcutaneous insulin.** The subcutaneous dose is given with a meal and the infusion is stopped after an overlap (here one hour), because IV insulin acts for only minutes; stopping it before the subcutaneous insulin is absorbed would let ketones rise again.

**Prevention.** Never stop insulin during illness; check glucose and ketones every few hours when unwell; keep up fluids, using sugar-containing drinks if unable to eat; seek help early for persistent vomiting, rising ketones or deep breathing; keep diabetes clinic follow-up.
quality_report: Drafted by Claude (ai:claude, 2026-10-10) from CASE_REQUEST NRG-MS-002 (primary domain NP, difficulty low, Q7 HPMW, Q8 NLM). Checks run on all eight items: Cover (each key can be formed before seeing options from the data on screen), Two-Answer (Q1 glucose vs pulse resolved by stem 'given Akeem's history' and the fluid already running; Q5 'reduce insulin' excluded by the stated protocol that insulin-rate changes need a prescription; Q8 options limited so only one task is routine and non-assessment), Cue-Sufficiency (Q3 asked before ketones/gas results; Q4 potassium 5.4 shown before planning; Q5 protocol authority given in the earlier 3:15 pm stage, not the 7:15 pm stage), Hidden-Assumption (protocol, weight, insulin regimen and potassium addition all stated before use; Q6 intervention introduced in the 7:15 pm and Day 2 stages). Disclosure: Kussmaul breathing and the fruity odour withheld until Q2 so Q1 is not pre-assembled. Addendum 3: urine output and electrolytes given at 3:15 pm, 7:15 pm and Day 2. Jade to confirm: (1) local DKA protocol - this case follows a UK JBDS-style fixed-rate infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr, insulin continued and 10% dextrose 125 mL/hr added when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL); ADA practice instead lowers the insulin rate with 5% dextrose, so the Q5 key depends on the protocol stated in the case; (2) potassium thresholds for adding KCl; (3) one-hour IV/subcutaneous overlap; (4) whether direct admission from a district health centre without prior ketone testing is realistic locally; (5) nursing assistant scope in T&T for intake/output recording and disconnecting IV lines; (6) sick-day ketone-check frequency (every 4 hours) and whether home blood or urine ketone testing is accessible to clients locally. Reviewer (2026-10-10): Admission potassium changed from 5.4 to 5.8 mmol/L (Q4 rationale, self-test and teaching section updated), because at 5.4 a JBDS protocol, which this case follows for insulin, would already add 40 mmol/L KCl, contradicting the Q4 key 'as the level falls'; at 5.8 both JBDS (no KCl above 5.5) and ADA (hold above 5.2) withhold KCl until the 5:30 pm repeat of 4.6, as written. Added to the 2:30 pm stage that the ward's ketone meter is on loan and has been sent for: a nurse acting on the Q1 cue would otherwise be expected to check ketones at the bedside before Q3, and the later hourly ketone checks need a meter. Q8 option D reworded from 'Decide whether Akeem needs a snack' (the word 'decide' gave it away) to 'Give Akeem a snack whenever Akeem reports feeling shaky', a more tempting unsafe distractor; rationale updated. Q7 option B retyped priority to incorrect (an incomplete plan, not a sequencing error). Teaching section no longer states the stomach illness as fact. No keys changed. Course checked against JBDS/ADA: 0.1 units/kg/hr; glucose fall about 58 mg/dL/hr and ketone fall about 0.9 mmol/L/hr are in the target range; pH 7.16, bicarbonate 9, ketones 5.6 is moderate, not severe, DKA, so ward care fits; Day 2 values meet resolution criteria. Jade to confirm: whether a urine ketone dipstick would routinely be done on a T&T ward before the blood results (it would weaken the 'before confirmation' design of Q3), plus the author's items (1) to (6). Revision (2026-10-12): Added home medications to the opening (NPH 18 units and regular 8 units before breakfast, NPH 8 units and regular 6 units before dinner, about 0.6 units/kg/day at 64 kg; no last-dose status, so the missed insulin still first appears at 2:30 pm) and the health-centre 0.9% sodium chloride. Charted orders where the narrative makes them: 0.9% sodium chloride, the 6.4 units/hr insulin infusion and the protocol 10% dextrose at 3:15 pm; insulin and the potassium-containing fluid (40 mmol/L, added 5:30 pm) at 7:15 pm, with the dextrose left off that chart so it does not cue Q5; dextrose 'running since 7:15 pm' only on Day 2, after Q5; the subcutaneous doses 'given 8:30 am' and the infusion 'to stop at 9:30 am' at 8:30 am. Added pain scores (4/10, 4/10, 1/10, 0/10), temperature and SpO2 where missing, and full eight-system examinations in order at 1:45 pm, 2:30 pm, 7:15 pm and Day 2 (normal systems written as normal; weakness, warm dry skin, faint breath odour at 7:15 pm consistent with ketones 2.4 mmol/L). Wording changes: the 2:30 pm findings (slower answers, fruity odour, clear chest) moved from the narrative into the structured examination so the cues sit among normals; the 3:00 pm capillary glucose moved from vitals to a 'Bedside tests' lab group. No stems, options or keys changed. Jade to confirm: the home insulin doses, the fluid rates (1 L over 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, 6 h) and KCl 40 mmol/L. Revision (nursing focus, 2026-10-12): Q3 rewritten as the priority nursing diagnosis; old key D 'Diabetic ketoacidosis', new key D 'Deficient fluid volume related to osmotic diuresis and vomiting as evidenced by a pulse of 118/min and a dry mouth' (distractors: ineffective breathing pattern, priority; risk for electrolyte imbalance, close; deficient knowledge, incorrect); new rationales, self-test and meta, still ASE. Q4 rewritten from an anticipated prescription to a nursing intervention for the priority problem; old key B 'Potassium chloride added to the IV fluid as the level falls', new key B 'Record intake and urine output hourly with pulse and blood pressure' (potassium now taught in the Q4 rationale and the teaching section). Q6 options rewritten to measure the nursing-diagnosis outcome; old key A 'Blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L with venous pH 7.35', new key A 'Pulse 86/min, moist tongue, urine output 70 mL/hr' (ketones/pH kept as a close distractor). Q5, Q7 and Q8 checked: nursing actions on the presentation, keys unchanged (C, D, B); Q5 key differs from Q4. Q1 key unchanged (C); its rationale and self-test no longer say the IV fluid already covers the pulse and dry mouth, which would have contradicted Q3. Removed 'strict fluid balance' from the 3:15 pm prescriptions so that stage does not hand over Q4's key; the physician's DKA diagnosis stays in that stage, after Q3. Objective and teaching section updated to name the priority nursing diagnosis and link Q4-Q8 to it. Flow rechecked: Q3 asked at 2:30 pm before results; Q6 evaluates IV fluid (opening) and hourly monitoring (Q4); no stage text repeats a key. Jade to confirm: deficient fluid volume over ineffective breathing pattern as the priority (Kussmaul breathing treated as effective compensation), hourly urine measurement without a catheter on a T&T ward, and whether 'strict fluid balance' should be restored as a physician order after Q4.
